title: The Alert Curve
primary_metric: confirmed real incidents per false escalation triggered -- Threshold Trip policy vs. Curve Check policy

options.A: Escalate now under the Threshold Trip -- the raw alert count this hour has already crossed the threshold
options.B: Hold for the Curve Check -- wait one more sampling interval and confirm the alert rate is truly accelerating before escalating

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC section 4

deliverables.text: A full symbolic derivation of dS/dt (the threat score's rate of change), using the chain rule, with the composite's outer function and inner function explicitly identified.
A full symbolic derivation of dA/dt (the alert rate's rate of change), using the product rule on A(t) = V(t) . S(t), substituting D1's chain-rule result for dS/dt.

A written justification, using the definition of differentiable, of why the raw minute-by-minute alert count cannot supply a true instantaneous rate of change, and why the continuous composite model A(t) can.
The equation of the tangent line to A(t) at the current sampling instant t0, using D2's dA/dt as its slope, and what that tangent line predicts for A at the next sampling instant.

A confirmed-incidents-per-false-escalation ratio for the Threshold Trip policy and the Curve Check policy, computed from the historical log by classifying each past interval under both policies' rules, with the percentage margin between the two ratios and a recommendation.

How To Math Questions To Research

balance.argument_a: The raw hourly alert count crossing the threshold is available immediately, with zero additional delay -- for any interval where a true accelerating attack does trip the threshold, the Threshold Trip policy escalates it exactly one sampling interval sooner than the Curve Check policy ever could, since Curve Check requires waiting for that next interval before its derivative confirmation exists at all. Every real incident that Curve Check would eventually confirm, Threshold Trip already caught earlier -- the only question is how many additional, non-incident alerts also crossed the threshold alongside them.
balance.argument_b: Because A(t) is a product of traffic volume and threat score, a pure volume spike with a flat or falling threat score can push the raw count over the threshold without dA/dt ever turning positive -- Curve Check's chain-and-product-rule confirmation filters exactly that case out, so every interval it does escalate carries a real, computed acceleration signal that Threshold Trip's raw count alone cannot distinguish from noise. If a large share of Threshold Trip's threshold crossings come from volume-only spikes, Curve Check's confirmed-incidents-per-false-escalation ratio beats Threshold Trip's by a wide margin, even after accounting for every real incident Curve Check catches one interval late.
balance.margin_basis: Confirmed real incidents per false escalation, computed separately for the Threshold Trip policy and the Curve Check policy from Appendix D's historical interval log, once Appendix C's threshold and sampling interval and Appendix A's function coefficients are sourced or accepted as Modeling Assumptions.
